theory.intro: Angles in a diagram often add up to a known total. Spotting the relationship lets you find a missing angle.
facts: Two angles forming a **right angle** add to $90^{\circ}$.
Angles on a **straight line** add to $180^{\circ}$.
Angles **at a point** (around a vertex) add to $360^{\circ}$.
steps: Decide which relationship the diagram shows ($90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$ or $360^{\circ}$).
Subtract from the total to find the unknown.

foundation.solution_text:
The arms form a square corner.
This is a **right angle**, so angles filling it total $90^{\circ}$.

The two outer arms make a straight line.
These are **angles on a straight line**, totalling $180^{\circ}$.

The sectors meet at one vertex and fill a full turn.
They are **angles at a point**, totalling $360^{\circ}$.

The two angles fill the corner between perpendicular arms.
They form a **right angle** and total $90^{\circ}$.

$m$ and $n$ share a vertex and their other arms point in opposite directions.
They are **angles on a straight line**, totalling $180^{\circ}$.

All four sectors meet at one point and complete a revolution.
They are **angles at a point**, totalling $360^{\circ}$.

development.solution_text:

The total is $90^{\circ}$.

A ruler edge is straight, and the two adjacent sectors sit above it.
They are **angles on a straight line**, totalling $180^{\circ}$.

Every sector surrounds the same post and together they make one revolution.
They are **angles at a point**, totalling $360^{\circ}$.

The sectors surround one common corner and fill a complete turn.
Use the **angles at a point** total, $360^{\circ}$.

mastery.solution_text: No. The three selected sectors extend below the straight line and do not form only a half turn. A known total applies only when the chosen sectors exactly fill the relationship.
$p+q=180^{\circ}$ is one valid relationship because together they lie along one straight path. (The pairs $q+r$, $r+s$ and $s+p$ are also valid.)
$A$, $B$ and $C$ do not exactly fill a right angle or half turn. With $D$, they form the full set of angles at a point, whose known total is $360^{\circ}$.
